name: KIT (white spotting)
summary: KIT, on chromosome 3, is a receptor that pigment cells need in order to survive and spread through the skin of the embryo. Its variants leave areas without pigment cells: white hair over pink skin, present from birth. It decides where pigment is, never whether that pigment is red or black, and every other colour gene still acts in the coloured areas. This locus holds sabino 1 (SB1) and the numbered W series - W1 to W39 in the published series, with no W29 or W36 - as alternatives at one position. They range from boosters that show little or nothing alone (W20, W32, W34, W35; W20 is in 25 of 28 breeds surveyed, at allele frequencies up to about a third in Thoroughbreds and Gypsy Cobs, and in Paint Horses W20 alone added only about one per cent of white), through sabino-like patterns, to all-white horses, and the same genotype can look very different on two horses. W4 is the Camarillo White variant. W17 is two missense changes that are always found together on one chromosome, from a Japanese Draft family; they were once listed as two alleles, W17a and W17b, which are kept only as invalid ids. Homozygotes are known and viable for SB1, W15, W19, W20, W32, W34 and W35; for the others none has been observed, and death of the embryo is suspected but unproven. W22 has only ever been found on a chromosome that also carries W20; UC Davis reports that chromosome as W20_22, and the W22 allele here stands for it. A horse can have W20 without W22, never W22 without W20. Real horses can carry other variants together on one chromosome too (W35 with W37, W19 with W34 and W35, W32 with W35, SB1 with W32), which a pair of alleles cannot express. Tobiano, an inversion near KIT, and roan, mapped to the KIT region with no causal variant known, are separate loci here. No effect on build, performance or temperament is established.

alleles.name: White spotting W22 (the W20_22 haplotype: a 1,898 bp deletion on a W20 chromosome)
Dominant white W17 (two missense changes on one chromosome: c.2001A>T, p.Glu667Asp and c.2021T>C, p.Leu674Pro)
White spotting W37 (frameshift insertion; candidate; found only with W35)
Dominant white W17a (invalid: one half of W17, never found alone)
Dominant white W17b (invalid: one half of W17, never found alone)

phenotypes.name: Little or no white
phenotypes.description: One copy of a booster - W20, W32, W34 or W35. Often no white at all, or only ordinary-looking markings; at most a sabino-like pattern. A solid-looking horse can carry one. Their main effect is to add white beside sabino 1, tobiano or a stronger W variant.

phenotypes.name: Sabino
phenotypes.description: One copy of sabino 1. Bold white on the legs, a wide blaze, white on the belly, and jagged or roaned edges. Variable: often flashy, not necessarily very white.

phenotypes.name: Sabino-like white
phenotypes.description: One copy of a W variant whose usual effect is a sabino-like pattern: irregular white on the legs, face and body. The amount varies a great deal between horses with the same variant, and W5 can be extensive. W22 here is the W20_22 haplotype: the deletion is always on a chromosome that also carries W20, so one W22 copy is also one W20 copy.

phenotypes.name: Sabino-like to all white
phenotypes.description: One copy of W6, W10, W15 or W38. Anything from a sabino-like pattern to an all-white horse. W38 is known from one family, with pink skin, small pigmented spots and sometimes blue eyes.

phenotypes.name: Boosted white
phenotypes.description: A booster (W20, W32, W34 or W35) beside sabino 1 or beside a W variant that is not all-white on its own. More white than the stronger variant gives alone; how much is not fixed. W20 with W5 can give an all-white or nearly all-white horse. W20 with W22 (two W20 copies, one of them carrying the W22 deletion) is usually all white; the paper that found W22 reported such horses as fully white.

phenotypes.name: Sabino-white
phenotypes.description: Two copies of sabino 1. At least 90 per cent white, and viable.

phenotypes.name: All white
phenotypes.description: White hair over pink skin across the whole body, from birth. Pigment cells never reached the skin, so the other coat genes the horse carries cannot be seen, though they are still inherited. One copy of an all-white W variant does this, with or without a booster beside it. Blue eyes can occur where the loss of pigment reaches the eye, and so much pink skin is sensitive to the sun.

phenotypes.name: Two copies, observed
phenotypes.description: Two copies of W15, W19, W20, W32, W34 or W35. Horses with these pairs have been observed and are viable. What they look like is not described.

phenotypes.name: Two copies, never observed
phenotypes.description: Two copies of the same W variant, where no such horse has been observed. The pair may be lethal to the embryo - most strongly suspected for W1 to W4 - but that is not proven for any of them: these variants are rare, and two carriers may simply never have been bred together.

phenotypes.name: Two different variants (not documented)
phenotypes.description: Two different variants for which no outcome has been described. Variants at this locus tend to add to each other, and horses carrying several have been found, but nothing can be given for this pair.

phenotypes.name: Nearly all white
phenotypes.description: One copy of W37 or W39. W39, known from a single mare, gives a nearly all-white horse with coloured hairs scattered through the body and head. W37 gives bold white on the legs, belly and face, up to nearly all white with small dark patches on the face, and sometimes a blue eye; every horse reported with it also had W35 on the same chromosome, so W37 beside W35 is the pair that has actually been seen.

phenotypes.name: Pair with an invalid allele
phenotypes.description: A pair that includes W17a or W17b. Those were once listed as two separate variants, but they are two changes always found together on one chromosome, which is the allele W17. They are kept, marked invalid, so that stored data still lines up and nobody adds them back. No outcome is given for them.
